rv.q: Overall, this is a well-crafted play that carries us efficiently to our inevitable destination, its placid surface rippled by rising passions.
It's not a radical or earthshaking show, but fans of stately period dramas with a feminist twinkle won't go away disappointed.

As such, I cannot urge you enough to go and see this intense and powerful drama which is hugely entertaining and speaks volumes about the quality of the source material and those who have been charged with bringing it to life.

The narrative ceases before Evans has actually adopted her legendary nom de plume. But playgoers by that point will surely be in thrall to the psychic journey that has led her to this decision … the play feels entirely modern in its insistence on the kind of self-reckoning that people talk about these days when they reference “being seen”.
Bird Grove is more enjoyable in its tightly written, and often humorous, often ironic, first half than in its second, which does meander a bit.
Too often, oafish suitors, awkward dinners and hackneyed cries of 'I want to read!' overwhelm the tender portrait of a complex domestic life that we see glimpses of throughout.
If this is truly Eliot's origin story, perhaps we're best left without it.
